utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. We're about to start a new witness. Is there a procedural matter before we do?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Before we start with the next witness, I wanted to raise one procedural matter. We would like to make an oral application to add a new exhibit to our exhibit list. This exhibit is a video that was brought by the witness last Thursday when he came for proofing. Mr. Stamp had referred to this issue last Friday when he made his submissions to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Has this been provided to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes. The video was disclosed last Friday. We only received it Thursday afternoon, and it was processed by our evidence unit Friday morning. And as soon as that was done, we provided it to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did receive two CDs or DVDs, I'm not sure what format it was, and one contains the footage purported to be by the witness of the location where allegedly there was a mass grave in Izbica, and the other recording pertains to something that is not in the indictment at all. It's Padalishte. As for the second recording, it is clear that the Defence contends that it cannot and should not be admitted into evidence in this case. As for the first recording, it is controversial because it is not clear why it is only after so much time has elapsed this recording now crops up, and it must be tendered through this witness. That is why the Defence objects to the admission of both those recordings. I've stated our reasons. In particular, the recording that might be relevant for the indictment, since it was only provided to us now, and it is quite strange in light of the witness's diligence in his events in his testimony in other cases so far that he never mentioned this recording. So the question of credibility and of whether he actually took the recording, this is all highly contentious, and that is why the Defence objects to the tendering of this exhibit. And my colleague Ms. Kravetz did not specify whether both recordings should be admitted or just one of the two. I would like clarification in this regard, and then I may take the floor again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may clarify the matter. I'm only referring to the new video that was provided to the Defence on Friday. This is 65 ter 05243. My colleague is correct that a second video was provided also on Friday. We indicated in the e-mail that went out when this was disclosed that this is a video that was only disclosed out of an abundance of caution. It relates to a statement which was disclosed in 2007, December 2007, to the Defence, and we do not intend to use the statement or that video. We're only disclosing it so the Defence has all the material relevant to this witness, but it is not a video that we intend to use with this witness. Now, as to the issue of why the new video was only provided to us by the witness at this stage, the issue of the witness having filmed this video only came up during his testimony in the Milutinovic case. At the time we were asked by Presiding Judge Bonomy whether we possessed a copy of the video; we indicated we didn't. We hadn't been provided a copy by the witness. When the witness returned back home, we asked him to send us a copy of the video. He looked for it back home. He didn't have a copy and he was unable to locate a copy. It is only recently that the witness has been able to locate a copy. The video was in fact back in Kosova at a brother's house, and the brother was able to locate the original of this video. From what I understand, the witness asked his brother to send him the video when he arrived last week here in The Hague, and we received it on Thursday and immediately provided it to the Office of the Prosecution. So this is the explanation we have received for the delay in providing this video to the Office of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is the relevance of the video to the case? Can you indicate that to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This video is directly relevant to the witness's observations he made at Izbica when he returned there in June 1999. He in fact filmed this video that month when he was there, and we believe it's going to better assist the Chamber in understanding his observations at the time. Specifically, it refers to the removal of the bodies from the graves at Izbica, and it just shows the conditions that the grave-site was at when the witness returned after the war was over in 1999. That is the relevance of the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And it's advanced on the basis that it is a video actually filmed by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes. The witness appears on the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That hasn't answered my question. If he appears on it, he can't film it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: From what I understand, he was being filmed and then he filmed a part of it. But I think the witness will be able to explain which part he filmed and who filmed the part where he appears on the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view, Ms. Kravetz, that the DVD that you are speaking of should be added to the Rule 65 ter witness list. The Chamber will, however, hear the witness and, if appropriate, view the video before deciding whether or not it should be received as an exhibit. We realise the list is primarily to give notice to the Defence and the Chamber that the Prosecution intends to use something. The question of admissibility is a distinct issue and the Chamber wishes to consider that in light of the evidence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. The next Prosecution witness is Mr. Liri Loshi. Mr. Loshi will be testifying to the allegations contained in paragraph 75(F) and Schedule F of the indictment and paragraph 77.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that Mr. or Dr.?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Dr. Liri Loshi, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation shown to you on the card.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Ms. Kravetz has questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Could you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Good morning. My name is Liri Loshi. The first name is Liri and the surname is Loshi.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When and where were you born, Mr. Loshi?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I was born in Padalishte on the 20th of August, 1960. It's in the municipality of Skenderaj in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Loshi, that you are a doctor by profession and that you are of Kosovo Albanian ethnicity. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I want to begin by asking you some questions of events that took place in the municipality of Skenderaj, or Srbica, in March of 1999. In the days preceding the NATO bombardment, that is, on the days before 24 March 1999, where were you living?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: During those days I was living in Leqina, and I was acting in this area: Leqina, Izbica, Turiqevc, Korenica, and the villages close to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Once the NATO bombing began on 24th March, did you remain in Lecina?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes. On the 24th of March, I was in Leqina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: At the time were you a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Since when had you been a member of the KLA, Mr. Loshi?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I became a member of the KLA after my house was burned in Padalishte and after I was expelled by the Serbian forces in the place where I was working, and for that reason I had to leave my village and went to live in Leqina. And it was at that time that I joined the KLA. It was around August 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You mention that your house in Padaliste was burned. When did this occur?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: My house was burned. It was burned by the Serbian forces. I don't know why. At that time I worked as a doctor. The Serb forces came to the village. They burnt my house first and then they burnt a couple of other houses. They expelled all the villagers from the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you told us that you left Padaliste and you went to Lecina. Did your family come with you to Lecina?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No, my family didn't because my family went to Mitrovica and from there to Prishtina. I was alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: By the time of the NATO bombing, had your family returned to live with you in the municipality of Srbica?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No. During the NATO bombardment, my family remained in Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And during that period, were you still practicing as a doctor?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What was your role within the KLA?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I did not have a specific role. I joined the KLA mostly because of safety reasons. I asked them to give me a gun so that I could survive. There were only two solutions in front of me: One was to leave the place; the other was to remain and be in danger of my life. And I chose the second, but I asked the KLA to give me a gun. At that time the condition was that they could supply me with a gun but I had to become a member of the KLA. That's how it happened, and I never regretted. I am proud that I was a member of that army, even today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were you ever engaged in any combat activity with the KLA, either in 1998 or in 1999?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No, I didn't participate in any combat activity. You asked me earlier what my tasks were or what my role was in the KLA. I did not have a specific task, but I was a doctor, a physician, and I took care of the civilians and the soldiers. So in fact, this was my main job, and whenever there were wounded people, I went as close to them as possible, to them so that I could give them first aid. It is impossible to go to the front as a doctor, but I always was in the rear. But as I said, I always took care of the civilians and the soldiers. At the same time I also reported for the Kosova Radio and Television, which was based in Tirana at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you told us that on the 24th March you were in the village of Lecina. Did you remain in the village of Lecina throughout the last week of March?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: On the 24th of March I was in Leqina; also on the 25th and the 26th I was in these villages. I left Leqina on the 26th, and I couldn't go back anymore, in the future, because the Serb forces started to shell the area so it would be very dangerous for me to enter Leqina. And that day, on the 26th, I remained in Izbica. A day earlier I visited the village of Korenica -- correction, Klodernice, where three people had been killed by the shelling from the village of Junik. Three people were killed in a house. That day, on the 25th of March, the population was concerned and they started to leave their houses. I went and visited the people wherever they were in the village of Klodernice, as I mentioned, where the people had gathered, and then I returned to Turiqevc where the clinic was, continued with my work there. I returned to Leqina on the 26th --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If I may stop you there just so we understand. So you left Lecina on the 26th of March; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you tell us that you went to Kladernica that day?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: On the 25th of March I went to Klodernice. The reason I discussed this at length is because on the 25th of March when I went to Klodernice, then after that I went to Turiqevc and then returned to Leqina. On the 25th I slept there, while on the 26th I left Leqina and went to Turiqevc, from Turiqevc returned to Izbica. By mid-day I was in Izbica and spent the whole day there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You told us that on the 26th of March the population was concerned and they start to leave their houses. Which population were you referring to, which of all these villages that you've been speaking about?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: As I said, on the 25th of March the population was really concerned and shocked by the killing of the innocent people that had happened, so they began to leave their houses because they thought they were not safe there anymore. In the beginning they started to gather in the school of Klodernice, and then some of them thought that it would be better for them to move to Izbica. So on the 26th of March the people from the -- from all the villages, a large group of people from Klodernice and other villages - Leqina, Vojnik, Kopiliq, Rakitnica, and other villages, all of them started to gather in Izbica because the place where they gathered was a kind of valley between two hills and they felt safer there from the shelling. The geographical arrangement was such that it would protect them from shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Dr. Loshi, you told us that you went to Izbica on the 26th of March. Why did you decide to go to Izbica that day?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: When I went to Turiqevc where the clinic was, there were no people there, no patients, so how could I stay there alone? There were some technicians, medical assistants who helped me there. We took some medical equipment and decided to go to Izbica, thinking that that would be a safer area for me and for the team that worked there. At the same time we also wanted to be close to the people. As I said, there was a large number of people there, about 25.000 of them. So the reason was, I wanted to be safe but also be close to the people who I could help in case of need.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You say that -- you said that there were about 25.000 people in Izbica. Where were these people staying?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: You mean where they were staying, where they were living that day?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, that day. I'm just asking you what the situation was like when you arrived in Izbica on the 26th of March.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] That day the people were in the valley close to the school. There is a school with four classrooms there. I think some of them were inside the school, but most of them were outside. As I said, there were large numbers of people. They were in the field, in the valley, all there, outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: For how long or for how many days did you remain in Izbica?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I stayed in Izbica on the 26th, I think only on that day. The next day, early in the morning, about 4.00 a.m., I left together with a friend. He was a doctor as well, Xhavit Dragaj. I took him in my car together with his family, and we went to Shik [as interpreted]. At this time the majority of the population began to leave towards the same direction, so -- I mean the direction from Izbica to Shik, because there was very heavy shelling on the Izbica village, and the fear was that the Serb forces would penetrate to Izbica very soon, so the majority of the people started to leave and go Tushile. And I did the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just to clarify the transcript, could you repeat the name of the village to where you headed when you left Izbica because I don't think it's in --

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes. Tushile.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's spelled T-u-s-h-i-l-e.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So you told us that the majority of the population also started to head in the same direction. Now, for how many days did you remain in Tusilje?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I went to Tushile on the 27th and I remained there the whole day of the 27th, also on the 28th. So in total I stayed there for two days. On the 29th I went to Kopiliq.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that there was heavy shelling in Izbica village or -- yes, that's how it's been written. When did the shelling begin?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: The shelling commenced on the 24th from the direction of Runik. Three people were killed in Klodernice village, as I mentioned earlier. The next days the forces came from the direction of Runik and to Leqina; this is on the 26th. And on the 27th they surrounded, they encircled, the village of Izbica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, these two villages that you referred to, Runik and Lecina, where are they located in relation to Izbica?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Runik is quite far, I would say about 4 or 5 kilometres, far away. Leqina is on the border. It's the first village near Izbica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you told us that you went to Tusilje on the 27th and stayed there on the 28th and that you later left for the village of Obilic. Could you explain why you went on the 29th to the village of Obilic?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes. As I explained earlier, when we went to Tushile, we went there because we felt safer there. We thought we were in danger at Izbica. We felt safe in Tushile for more or less two days because there wasn't any shelling at that time. So our security depended on the shelling that we would hear from the distance. So from the shelling we could tell approximately where the Serbian forces were at the time of the shelling. So on the 29th the noise of the shelling increased and we got the impression that the Serbian forces were very near. So on the 29th in the evening, which was the best time for movement as we could not be seen by the Serbian forces, I left for the direction that I used earlier to go to Izbica. But this time I didn't go to Izbica; I went a little bit to the right side up to the village of Kopiliq i Eperm, because the Serbian forces had already burned that part, had removed the civilian population. They had killed cattle, people, burned the houses. So their axis of movement now was in the direction of Tushile. So I was going in the opposite direction compared to them, to the area where I had been earlier, which they had already destroyed and burnt.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you told us that on the day that you left Izbica the population also started moving out because of this shelling. Do you know if anyone remained in Izbica, or did all the population leave on that same day?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I left Izbica very early in the morning, as I said, at around 4.00 a.m. My impression at the time was that most of the people were leaving. When I went there in the morning, I had the impression that there were about 2.000 or 3.000, up to 4.000 people. The rest of the people that I saw there this morning, they moved at the same time in the same direction as we did; some on vehicles, although there were not that many cars; some on tractors; and the majority of people were leaving on foot from Izbica to Tushile. So I met these people en route and, therefore, I believe that on that day about 3.000 or 4.000 people remained in Izbica. But as I said earlier, there were many, many, about 25.000 before, when I went there on the previous occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you told us that on the 29th you had been moving around and that you arrived to the village of Obilic. For how many days did you remain in Obilic?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I spent one night in Kopiliq, so one day and one night. I spent the night in a house there in Kopiliq. There, I came across some KLA soldiers, and this was by accident because the houses were burnt. I was there with this friend of mine who was also a doctor, and there was a teacher. This house that we went to belonged to this teacher. There, we met these KLA soldiers. Shaban Dragaj was there, too. I mentioned him several times. He was a chief of brigade, of the KLA brigade. This is where I saw him, and with him I went to Izbica and Vojnik on the following day. What I wanted to add here is that during this day, on the 30th of March -- so I went there on the 29th in the evening. On the 30th, during the day, I saw the Serbian forces in the direction of Tushile forcing the civilian population out of their houses to the asphalt road, Skenderaj-Kline road. Part of the population went back in the direction of Kline, while the other part in the direction of Skenderaj. This I saw from the village of Kopiliq. In the meantime a tank, military tank, passed by from Turiqevc to the direction of Runik. I was very close. I saw this tank from a close distance, I would say 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just to clarify something here. You said that on the 30th of March you saw Serbian forces in the direction of Tushile forcing the civilian population out of their homes. From where were you observing this?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I was in Kopiliq i Eperm on a hill, and from there you can see freely what is going on. I had binoculars, too. I could see the movement with the naked eye, but it was much better using the binoculars. So I could see the Serbian forces moving from Tushile in the direction of Rakitnica, a village by the asphalt road. And they were directing people, some in the direction of Skenderaj and some others in the opposite direction, that is, in the direction of Kline.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you say you saw Serbian forces, who exactly did you see directing people in these different directions?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Those that I saw were mixed. They were mainly military forces wearing greenish uniforms, and there were also Serbian forces that were dressed in uniforms, greyish uniforms. But the military forces were dominant because this is what I remember, the military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you also referred to having observed a tank passed by Turicevac. From where were you observing this when the tank passed?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: From the same location. I saw the tank early in the morning, at approximately 6.00 or 7.00 in the morning. The tank was moving from the direction of Turiqevc in the direction of Runik. It was only one tank, and the noise of another tank could be heard. I suppose that a tank was broken and that this one that I saw was going there as help, as assistance. It wasn't an attack or anything, but personally I feared that they would come to our direction because there were KLA soldiers there. I thought that they would come to the houses -- to the house up there where we were, but they didn't. They proceeded in the direction of Runik.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that in Obilic you met Shaban Dragaj, a KLA commander, and that you went to Izbica. Why did you decide to return to Izbica on the 30th of March?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I decide to go back to Izbica because I had an information that the Serbian police -- forces, correction, committed a massacre there. I received this information while I was at Tushile. A group of women came there, and I spoke to them as a doctor and as a human being, so I spoke to these women, and they told me that the Serbian forces had entered Izbica on the 28th and that they had separated the men, all the men that were there, those that were above the age of 14. Some of the women said that they, the Serbian forces, had asked the children for their age. They had only separated those who were above 14 years old, and people who were above 14 were mainly elderly people, civilians, so they separated them from the women and the children. And according to the story of this woman, whose father-in-law was taken by the Serbs, the group of women and children was made to leave in the direction of Turiqevc, and from there they were directed further to the direction of Kline. It is a small town. It's another municipality. It's about 12, 13, or 15 kilometres far. So this woman was telling me that when they separated the men, the women start to move in the direction of Turiqevc, and they could no longer join the direction where the men were taken. So this woman had heard gun-shots and she was under the impression that they had all been executed. And she said that her father-in-law was probably executed, too, so I asked her, What do you think about the number of people who were probably executed there? And she said, Around 100 or even more. I just hope that this didn't happen, that this massacre didn't happen, or in case it happened, that the number of the people executed was much smaller.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Before we move further, I would like to have Exhibit 00615 up on the screen, and I would like page 17.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, we're going to look at a map, just so we understand where all these villages that you've been referring to are located.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Before you look at this, I was quite emotional and did not finish my answer to your question because you asked me as to why I went to Izbica. So my answer is that I went to Izbica just to verify whether this information was true, whether these people were killed. So I just wanted to go there to verify this information, to see how these people were killed, if they were killed, and to take notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So could we have 00615. Oh, I don't have anything on my screen. It's not appearing on my screen. I'm sorry. Could we zoom in to the top right-hand corner. There, it's now on my screen. I apologise, Your Honours. If we could zoom in on the top right-hand corner of page 17. If we could zoom in where the village of Srbica appears, further down.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir, are you able to see the map on your screen?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I wonder if the usher could assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: There's a pen on the side of your screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If the usher could kindly assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I would like you to draw --

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I have a pen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is a special pen. Please don't write with your pen on this screen.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. Yeah. [Interpretation] No, no, I won't use it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So could you draw a circle around the village of Izbica, just so we see where it is.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you referred to making -- observing the Serb troop movement and a tank from Obilic. Could you draw a 1 where the village of Obilic is?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Let me find it first. It's here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you draw a number 1 next to that, sir, please.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, could you indicate where you saw the tank and the troops, in which direction you saw them moving, just with an arrow.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: So from Turiqevc, which is here, in the direction of Runik. So Turiqevc is here. They were moving in this direction. Runik is quite far. So this is the route which might be asphalted now, but at the time it was with gravel. So this is where I saw the tank, and it was moving in the direction of Runik. I'll mark it with an arrow. Here is the tank, moving from Turiqevc, so I could see it from here, from Kopiliq, and it was moving in the direction of Runik. I've marked this route with a straight line. Perhaps the road is here, so the tank should have been closer to Kopiliq. You can see the turn here. I've marked the direction with a straight line, but the route is denoted on the map. You can see it there. So my line represents just the direction, not the road itself. I don't know if I'm clear or not. If I'm not clear, please ask me and I will clarify.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So the tank was moving north from Turiqevc up to Runik, on the road that we see on the --

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. You're right. It was moving towards north.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we have an exhibit number assigned to the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're tendering this, are you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00287, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir, you told us why you returned to Izbica on the 30th of March. What did you find there once you returned that day?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: When I returned to Izbica, I saw the bodies lying at the place where they were executed. I stayed there for a very short time. It was dark, but I could see that my fears came true, that there was a large number of people, which had been calculated as about a hundred or over a hundred, that had been killed. So I verified and I could see that the massacre had really happened and there was a large number of people lying on the ground at the place where they were executed. And then I withdrew. I just had a look at what had happened and went to my patients, and then I rested until the next day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What did you decide to do once you discovered that there were bodies there in Izbica?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Well, as a doctor I saw that I could not help the executed people, but as a journalist I thought that I could record the massacre so that I could show the public opinion what had happened so that they would learn about the massacre committed by the Serb forces in Izbica. This is what I decided, but unfortunately I did not have a camera. When I left Leqina on the 26th in the morning, I left my camera over there because I thought I could go back, my personal camera. So I did not have a camera with me. I did not dare to go back for safety reasons, but I discussed the thing with Demush Dragaj and Shaban, where I stayed in Demush Dragaj's house; I was staying at that time, I mentioned it. Naim Rexhepi was the head of the village, civilian head of the village, and we discussed how could we find a camera so that we could record the bodies the next day. Demush said that he could find a camera, and he told me that his brother-in-law from Turjan - his name is Sefedin Thaqi - he had hidden his camera together with some other things underground. He had made a hole in the ground and had put these things in there. And Demush knew about this, from Sefedin Thaqi had done, so he took it upon himself to find it and take the camera, and we would go and record the massacre on the 20 -- correction, on the 31st of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were you able to return the next day to film these bodies?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: In the evening I went to see my patients; then also in the morning I went to see some of my patients. I only had a couple of patients who had been wounded in Izbica. Those were all the patients I had, so this did not take me a long time. And then after that I went to Izbica early in the morning on the 31st of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what did you do when you went to Izbica on the 31st of March?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: When I went to Izbica, Sefedin Thaqi himself had come with his camera and he had started recording. And I was very happy about that because the promise that had been given last -- the previous night that we would have a camera had come true. The person was there; he had started recording. We went to all the bodies. I gave instructions because I myself could not do the recording, all of it. I just gave him instructions what to record because I wanted to have a cassette that would document everything, which then would be completed with the conversations I would have with the survivors of the massacres and other information I would have later. So that's how it happened. I gave instructions to Sefedin and he went on recording. I returned -- went back, and then I contacted him later in the day. He continued recording during the whole day. I did have -- I did have a lot to do during that day. There were some patients of mine who were chronicle -- chronic patients, who had chronic illnesses, and some people who were wounded. I met some people whose relatives had been killed in the massacre, so I had to deal with them first.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And where were these bodies discovered, the bodies that you and Sefedin Thaqi filmed?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: The bodies were in two large groups. One group was immediately -- as you enter the village, there is a big field in Izbica, in the eastern direction, while the other one was about 800, 900 metres away from the first group, in the western direction. So these were the places were the recording was made. Then recordings were made, also, of the place where the civilian population was staying before they were forcefully expelled by the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would like to play a short clip, and this is 65 ter number 00232. If we could have that up on the screen. If we could ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you have that up on your screen, sir?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could stop right there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognize these images?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can you explain what was just shown there on our screen, what was depicted in these images?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: This depicts the group that was in the western direction. It is a large group of people. I can't remember the exact number, but there were at least 40 bodies there. I never counted the bodies myself; I think I've said that earlier. As you can see, they were very close to each other and they were all elderly people. I think there was a young man under 30 years old in that group. I think he was deaf. Well, as you can see from the pictures themselves, these people had sticks that helped them to walk. They were invalids; they were not able to move normally or walk normally. And it was exactly these people who were executed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What would you say was the average age of the victims that you -- that we just saw on the screen, that were found at this location?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I'm not exactly sure but about 60 to 80 years old, so an average of 70 years old. There was a woman there who was born in 1911, so their birthdays were 1920's or so. Maybe the average age was 70 years old. That's what I could say. Only a few of them were younger.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said there was also a woman in this group that was found there.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No. I said it wrong. This woman was burned in a tractor. It was down in the village where the people had been forced to leave out. This woman could not move. She was in a tractor, and the Serb forces just set the tractor on fire and she was burned alive in the tractor. But there was no woman in that group that was executed there now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could see a second clip now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we also play a third clip.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Dr. Loshi, did you recognize those images that we just saw on the screen?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes. This is, again, in Izbica but the opposite direction. This is the group that was in the eastern direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And are these images also images of the video that you and Mr. Thaqi filmed?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were you able to recognize any of the victims either in this group that we saw here or the other ones that were found in the western direction?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes. I knew a great number of those people. I have forgotten their names now because they used to be my patients and I knew their names and surnames. Now, with the passing of time, I've forgotten some of the names but some I can remember. Some of the people in the group were my relatives and they remained unidentified until the 1st of April, because the funeral happened on the 31st of March and 1st of April, but my relatives had remained there because nobody had identified them. It was Selman Jashari, and Sami Loshi. Selman Jashari was Jashar's father, and Jashar was Sami's father. So three generations from the Padalishte family, they died there. In the other group, the one in the eastern direction --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: May I stop you there just to clarify the names. You said there were three generations. One person was called Selman Jashari; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No, just Selman. His son was Jashari. Their surname is Loshi, so Selman Loshi, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Oh, so, this is correct: It's Selman Loshi; his son is Jashar?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And the last name is Loshi. And his son, what was his name?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Sami, his first name was Sami. Selman was over 80 years old, Jashar was about 55, and the other one, about 25 years old. I mean Sami, Jashar's son.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What sort of injuries were you able to observe on these bodies, the bodies found in these two large groups?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: These were wounds that are created, of course, by firearms at close distance with projectiles of large caliber, because these were very large wounds on their faces, bodies, hands, arms and legs. Wherever they were caught by the projectiles, the wounds were irregular and very large. So my opinion at that time was that they were killed at close range by projectiles of very large caliber. We also saw cuts on the bodies. On Sami's face, I saw some cuts. I don't know whether they were caused after the massacre or during the massacre, but there were cuts on his face. So in addition to being killed by bullets, he had cuts on his face. There were other cases now and then where we saw cuts made by knives or razors.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And of the bodies that you were able to observe, were any of them dressed in any sort of military uniform or military attire?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No. In the groups that we found, there were none of them that had military uniforms on. Everybody was a civilian. In the funeral, I saw one body wearing a uniform of the KLA, and I understood then that this was Ajet Beqiri who had been killed a day before the massacre together with Beqiri, on the 27th of March. There were no other bodies in uniform in these groups. While Ajet, who was in uniform, and Zaim, who was killed together with him, they were members of the KLA, Zaim was a nurse, and he used to work with me. At the time he was wearing civilian clothes; however, he was a member of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And where were these two persons killed, the ones that you just referred to, Ajet and Zaim Beqiri?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: They were killed far from the place of the massacre, maybe 1 kilometre away. I did not make any measurements as such, but I know that he was killed close to his home. He was at his home with Ajet, and they went out, probably, to see where the forces were. And when they went up the hill, there was a police or military check-point, a check-point of the Serb forces anyway, so they had been seen and killed by them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you told us at the beginning of your testimony that at the time you were a member of the KLA. To your knowledge, were any of those people that were killed on the 28th of March members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Are you speaking about the groups of people that were killed? No, no, there weren't any, except for these two people that I mentioned. But these two people were killed a day earlier and were not in the groups that were executed at that place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would like to show you a third clip.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could play the -- a fourth clip, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could stop that there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognize these images?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes. This is the area where the civilian population had gathered. I can hear this noise. Is the footage stopped? Can I speak?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, the footage has stopped.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] So this was the location where the civilian population had gathered to on the 26th of March and the 27th of March, a location where about 20.000 to 25.000 people had sheltered and where 3.000 or 4.000 people remained, refugees, internally displaced people. So this is the area where the men had been separated from the women and children and were directed to two different directions, east and west, and were executed. So the women and children were not allowed to remain on this area but were directed to the directions I mentioned earlier. And in the meantime, as you can see from the images, they destroyed tractors and cars; they burnt them. They burnt everything they found there. This is where the woman that I mentioned was burnt on a tractor, and a woman from the neighborhood of Dragaj in Leqina was also killed in this location. I never learnt about the circumstances of her killing, but for the other woman, I know that she died because she was burned in the tractor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the woman that was burned in the tractor?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes. Her name is Ajmone Citaku. I think she was born in 1911 from the notes that we made. I think she was about 81 or so at the time. You can tell -- I think she was born in 1911. She is on the list that I gave the ICTY investigators. She is in the list of the people who were executed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, we saw images of a woman at the beginning of this clip. Is this a different woman than the one you're just referring to, or is it the same person?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No. It's a different woman. The woman that was burned was not recorded because she was burnt. The woman that you saw now is also from Dragaj neighborhood. She was much younger, as you can tell from the images. I'm not sure about her name, but I think she was called Zade Dragaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we now look at another additional clip.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And the next clip, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we stop that there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir, could you explain what was happening there in those images we just saw?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: After the graves were opened, the bodies were placed inside, and the images depict the covering of the bodies with earth. This is the day when we buried the bodies of the victims of the massacre at Izbica, so the recording and the burial took part on the same date, 31st of March. So everybody was working. They were bringing the bodies from the location where they had been killed to the location of the graves, and some others were opening the graves. And as you can see now, some are now covering those graves with earth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And these are, again, images of the video that you and Mr. Thaqi recorded; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes. The same tape, the same day, the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how many persons were buried that day in Izbica?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but more than 100, the majority of the bodies. Maybe 120, but I'm not sure how many were buried on that day, because several people, my cousins and some others, remained there unburied because they had not been identified since their relatives were not there to identify them on the 31st of March. So their relatives were expected to come and identify them on the 1st of April. I believe there were seven or eight buried the following day, on the 1st of April, 1999, but I know the total number of the two days of people who were buried. On the 31st of March and 1st of April, a total of 127 bodies were buried, and we compiled the list. This is the list with the names of those who were buried on these two dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Who compiled the list of names of those who were buried?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: We formed a council, burial council, consisting of Afrim Xhemajli, Sadik Xhemajli, and some other people from the village of Izbica. The list itself was compiled by Afrim Xhemajli, who at the same time took care of the location where the people would be buried so that in the future in case things got mixed up, people would know who was buried where, and so that people later on after the war and after Kosova was liberated could come back to the location and rebury their dearest. So this is the method used in compiling the list. It follows the line. There are three columns on the list and each corresponds to the line of the graves in Izbica. Afrim Xhemajli was responsible for the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir, were the graves marked in any way so that they could later be identified?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: To my recollection, yes. They were recorded on a wood plank, so the name of the person and where he was from and the year of birth. Maybe not all of them had their year of birth placed on the wood plank, but the names were there. One remained unidentified, but later on he was identified. I don't remember his name. This is the person who was deaf that I mentioned earlier. At the time, we didn't know his name, but later on this information was provided.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir, on the images we just saw, we saw persons in uniform. Who were these persons?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I only saw one person. I remember his name. His name was Avdi. He was a KLA member. I don't recall seeing any other member. Maybe there were, but this is whom we saw. He was a tall man, he was dressed in uniform, his name was Avdi, and he was a KLA member. As I said earlier, there might have been other members of the KLA there who were working together with the villagers on the day of the burial so that they could bury their close ones, too. Let me explain. At the time there were not so many people in Izbica, maybe a total of 40 or 50 people, so those soldiers who were there were also obliged to help with the bodies; to carry them, to dig up graves, and to do all the work related to the funeral. And they had relatives among the victims, so a soldier would come to identify his father or his uncle or his brother and so on, and then bury his family member.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see we're approaching the time for the break. Just before we break, I would like to tender into evidence this video. It's 65 ter number 00232.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's all one DVD, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: It's one. We've seen clips of it, but it's just one DVD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00288, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, there are a series of still photos of these videos that accompany the video. These are 65 ter 00230 and 65 ter 00231, which I'm not going to go through with the witness but I wish to tender at this time. They're just still photos from the video that we just played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is the point of the still photos?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: They just assist in viewing the video and specifically identifying some of the victims there. We didn't play the video in its entirety, but some of the victims of this massacre which are listed in our schedule are identified in the video. And it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Whose identified them? Some other witness or this witness or what?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Who's going to -- I was just going to get to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We wish to also tender a portion of this witness's statement that contains the transcript for this video. This is 02436.02. The reason for this is that the transcript explains image by image what is happening and identifies -- indicates where the different victims are identified, those that appear in the video itself. And we consider that this will -- this portion of the statement will assist Your Honours in viewing the video and understanding what is happening. The transcript also contains a column which indicates the still photo that refers to the specific image, so Your Honours can compare the video with the transcript and the photos and actually understand -- or better understand what is taking place in the images that are played in the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to ask the Trial Chamber to stick to the order that has been envisaged, that the exhibits are first shown to the witness and then tendered into evidence. The reason -- well, there are several reasons, and if we're talking about a list that explains who can be seen on what recording, then there will probably be questions about who made the list, who produced it, and so on. And that is why I would kindly ask that the evidence be tendered into evidence after it is shown to the witness, nothing else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, is the identification made by the doctor in any of this film footage and his statement challenged by the Defence? Is it disputed?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence does not want to challenge that at this point in time. The Defence will clear this up through its cross-examination. We will not be challenging this, but this is a procedural objection. I thought that it was better for the evidence to be tendered into evidence only after they were shown to the witness. That's what I wanted to say, Mr. President, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber will adjourn now so that counsel can discuss what is now proposed. As I understand it, the video, having been shown, or most of it, the Prosecution now wishes us to receive both some still shots taken from the video and a part of the original statement of Dr. Loshi in which he identifies bodies that are shown in the film footage. Now, if his identification of those bodies is not disputed, it could well save quite a lot of time if we proceed as Ms. Kravetz is suggesting. On the other hand, if you are disputing the identification of those bodies, we might have to be much more particular. So could you and Ms. Kravetz discuss over the break how we might most efficiently proceed to deal with this identification evidence. And we will have our first break now and resume at five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. While the witness is being brought in to the court, I just wanted to indicate that I consulted with my colleague from the Defence during the break, and from what I understood, he has no objection to us tendering the still photos, so I seek to tender those and the video at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that, Ms. Kravetz, to you and to Mr. Djordjevic, and if you could proceed accordingly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we have an exhibit number, then, for the three exhibits, the video and the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you indicate for the record what they are --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- the three that you seek to tender?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The video is 65 ter 00232, and the sets of still shots are 00230 and 00231. Thank you. I seek to tender those at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's the video we've already received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P00288, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now the still shots, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first one with 65 ter 00230, Your Honours, will be P00289, and the next one identified as P00 -- as 00231 would be assigned P00290, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, as for the transcript of the video, the agreement that was reached was that I would show it to the witness and have him identify it prior to tendering it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So could we please have 65 ter 02436.02 up on the screen. Has that appeared? I don't have anything on my screen yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognize the document that is before you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes, I recognize it. This is a document that was compiled by the investigator of the Tribunal; Malvin Dagsland, I think was his name. He asked me to give my comments to him by listening to the tape. However, the description is his, but now and then I helped him with the description. The description was based on the photographs as we saw them. I helped him with the identification of bodies, the small number of people that I was able to identify. Also, when I heard people on the tape saying the name of a person that they identify, for example, Hetem Tahi, I helped him with that. However, if you asked me today, Who is Hetem Tahi in these photographs, I might not be able to recognize the person. So the column that says "Descriptions," I am responsible for -- sorry, this column that says "Comments," I am responsible for that one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just to clarify, we see there on the screen one that says -- the first entry there says, "Recorded on tape," and then we have Hetem Tahi's name. This was information that you were listening to when the video was being played, if I understood you correctly, and that you were providing to the investigator, so that would be included in this chart? Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That was the comment I made on Hetem Tahi. I think I recognised him because of the fact -- let me see grey jacket, grey cardigan. I'm not sure whether he had a walking stick or not to help him walk. But I did give him in name, yes. However, I'm not sure whether I recognized him at the time or I heard somebody mention his name on tape. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I need some further assistance, Ms. Kravetz. The second column appears to identify different photos by progressive numbers. Where are the photographs with those numbers?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: These are the still shots that I referred to earlier that I just tendered into evidence. As I explained earlier, the reason we seek to tender this transcript is precisely so Your Honours can match the video, because the first column has the frame with the minutes of the video, the second column has the photos, and then there's the description. So Your Honours can -- it's just to assist Your Honours in following the video and the different persons that are identified on there as being victims of this incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Progressively, then, it is the images seen on the exhibit video or DVD, progressively, it's each of the images of bodies that are seen on that film separately on a still shot with a separate number, which is shown on this list, and then there is a description and occasionally a comment that the name is unknown or another comment in the right-hand column.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the extreme left-hand column is the timing progressively through the filmed images.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will receive that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P00291, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we now have 65 ter 02436.01 up on the screen. Should I repeat the number? It's 02436.01. Could we enlarge the original version of this document for the witness on the screen so he can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, are you able to see the document there before you on your screen?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognize it?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: This is the list compiled by Afrim Xhemajli. I asked him to give me the list and he did give me the list when I left for Albania, together with a video-tape. On the left you can see the typed-up version of the list, while on the right you see the list that was hand-written by Afrim Xhemajli. You can see the people there given numbers. The first column represents the first row of graves and the people buried in that order. The second column is the second row, and the third column, the third row. I explained earlier why we did this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I think you may have already explained this earlier, but just to clarify, how were the different victims identified, the different persons who appeared on this list?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Well, for practical reasons, on the first column you have the names of the people who were buried in the first row. And I can't remember the order the people were buried, but I think the first row had 48 graves. The people could identify the victims once again after the war, if need be.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sorry, if I may interrupt you there. Maybe I should be clear on my question. Who identified the victims? Who provided the names?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: The victims were identified by their relatives, the relatives of the people who lay killed there. If, by any chance, no relatives were present, then people who knew them identified them, such as friends or acquaintances, but most of the people were identified by relatives or family members.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit at this stage. This is 02436.01.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00292, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Loshi, you have already explained what happened on the 31st and 1st of April when these persons were buried. For how long did you remain in Izbica after the funeral took place?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: After the funeral took place, I stayed there for about three or four days, and then I wanted to leave Izbica together with the tape. I went towards Llausha and then from there to Prekaz, and then I reached Cicavica, which is a village, early in the morning. Half an hour later, the Serb forces surrounded the village so I had to leave. And that was when I realised that the whole area I had passed through had been surrounded by the Serbs. So I traveled for four more days, mainly at night. During the day, I hid in the valleys or whenever I could. Then I had to return to Izbica because I couldn't get any further. I left Izbica on the 4th or 5th of May; I can't remember the exact date. But at that time I went to Albania. So in Izbica, I stayed for about a month after the massacre, with the exception of those four or five days when I attempted to leave but I couldn't leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What did you do with the tape that we just viewed earlier?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: The tape we watched earlier, that is an original tape we recorded on the 31st of March and 1st of April. Three or four days later -- well, of course, the tape was in the hands of the owner of the camera, and I think he wanted to keep the camera and the tape in order to make other private recordings. So later I asked him if he could give me the tape so that we could record from his tape into a bigger VHS cassette. That's what we did. We found an electric generator on the 4th of April, I think. I took this VHS cassette, while the other cassette was in his camera. Then he went to Albania and left the camera and the cassette in a hole in the ground, while the big cassette, the VHS one, was with me and I took that to Albania with me. I wanted to give it to somebody, but I couldn't contact anyone because it was a very difficult time. The Serb forces had occupied Drenice. Everywhere there were Serb forces and I couldn't meet anyone. A month later when I decided to leave for Albania, I heard that Sefedin Thaqi had left his camera where he had hidden it before. At that time I personally was living at his house together with Demush Dragaj. That was his son-in-law --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you, just for the sake of time, to be brief in your answers and concentrate on the questions I'm asking. Now, you've told us that you went to Albania in early May, after spending about a month in Izbica. What did you do with the tape, the one that we viewed today?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I was trying to explain how I took Sefedin's tape, because I looked for it and I found the camera and the cassette. I took the smaller cassette where he made the original recording on and I took it with me. I watched it again, and I saw that it had on it most of the recording that we had made that day. Part of it had been erased because he had recorded on it, but most of the tape was intact. So I took it to Albania. My cassette, I left it in Istog's mountains, and it would be dangerous for me to take it with me. It was too big to take away with me, so I went to Albania with a smaller cassette and I took it to the provisional Kosovo government, which was based in Tirana at the time. I handed it over to them in order for them to distribute it to the major international institutions, and that's what they did. One copy was sent to the White House, one copy to NATO, and I gave a copy to CNN. Several copies were made. I gave a copy to CNN, but then later I gave copies to BBC and other media. On the 19th of May I handed over the original cassette to the ICTY in their office in Tirana, while the larger VHS cassette remained in the mountains of Istog under the care of a villager there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you said you handed copies to several persons, including the press. Do you have any idea whether your video was broadcasted at the time by the press?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes, it was broadcast by various media. I remember two interviews I had with CNN personally, and CNN broadcast them by mid-May, 14th or 15th of May. James Rubin, who was the spokesman for the White House at the time, also held a press conference on this video-tape. I also think that NATO's spokesman held a press conference as well on the topic of this cassette.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, did you return to Kosovo once the war was over?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes, I did return. The war ended on the 10th of June when NATO forces entered Kosova. At that time my family was in Albania, in Tirana. I returned to Kosova on the 22nd of June. I returned alone. My family remained in Tirana.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did you return to the village of Izbica?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes. On the second day after I arrived, I went to Izbica. I went to Drenice, to the areas where I had been earlier. I saw some villagers, how they were returning to their villages. I saw the houses that had been burned down and I also saw that the Serb forces had withdrawn, were not there any longer. I went to Izbica because I had heard that the Serb forces sometime in May, by the end of May, had entered Izbica and had taken the bodies with them. So I wanted to go and see with my own eyes what was left there to see and record. I went there with a camera and recorded the place where the massacre had occurred, where the burial had taken place on the 31st of March and 1st of April, 1999, and then where I found the bodies that had been raised by the Serb forces. I also recorded people who described the situation to me. This was done on the 23rd of June by mid-day, sometime around mid-day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just going back a little, you said that you went to Izbica because you had heard that the Serb forces had exhumed the bodies. Who did you hear this from, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: When I was in Albania, I stayed at the office of the Kosova Radio and Television in Tirana, and we heard that information there. I'm not sure who said that first, but I heard that it was said there. On the 22nd of June, I entered Kosova, and on the 23rd when I went to Izbica, the villagers, all of them told me that the Serb forces had entered the area and had exhumed the bodies and taken the bodies to Serbia. I can't remember a name now because everybody was speaking about that at the time. I did not take down any notes about the names of people who were giving me this information. It was an information that was known by all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I wish to play another video, and this is the new exhibit that we were discussing at the beginning of the session. It's 05243, and it's just a clip from that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We can see the next -- the following clip, as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognize those images, Mr. Loshi?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes. These are the images I spoke about, images that I recorded with my own camera in July -- in the 23rd -- on the 23rd of June, 1999. This is the image and the recording of the razed graves. You could see bits and pieces left there, such as wood planks and other wooden objects where the names of the persons had been written. They had taken the bodies and then tried to raze and -- level the land. You could see the gloves that the Serb forces had used while exhuming the bodies and then taking them away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When we watched the video earlier of the funeral, we saw where the bodies had been buried. Just to clarify, is this the same location we saw earlier or is this a different location?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: It is exactly the same location. So we saw the burial site in the beginning, but now these graves are not there in their usual shape. The bodies have been removed and the ground has been leveled. So there are no graves there anymore in the last image we saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know or have any information as to where these bodies were taken?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I don't have an exact precise information. The villagers saw them removing the bodies. Some said that they were taken in the direction of Skenderaj, some in the direction of Mitrovica, some in the direction of Kline. These are all words that I heard from villagers. It is possible that these bodies were taken to all these directions, but that I don't know. I received this information from the villagers. So some said they were taken in the direction of Kline and some others in the direction of Skenderaj, which are two opposite directions. However, it is possible that the Serb forces took these bodies to both directions because there were many bodies there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you told us earlier that among the victims there were three of your relatives, and you've given us their names. Were the bodies of your relatives ever recovered?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: These bodies were removed together with the other bodies. I left Kosova, and in these ten years since this occurred I don't have much information. I think just one body was found, Sami's body, but again, I'm not sure whether it was recovered or not. But I don't know the location where it was recovered. Some of the bodies were found in Serbia; some were found in other parts of Kosova. So the bodies of the victims of Izbica were taken to different locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you told us that you filmed these images we saw -- just saw in June of 1999. Where has this video-tape been for the last nine -- nine-and-so years?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I made many recordings. When I entered Kosova, I stayed there for ten days. Part of my documentation remained with my brother in Kosova. He lives in Mitrovica now. When I came to The Hague, I requested that this tape to be delivered to me here. So I found a way for them to bring me the tape here. And this tape had not been given to the Tribunal or any other person or organisation until now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when did you get it back from your brother? You said when you came to The Hague, but when did that happen?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I received it in The Hague last Thursday. I don't remember the date, but it was last Thursday that I received it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit - it's 05243 - into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received -- sorry, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I was opposed to the admission of this evidence because it goes beyond the summary of this witness's evidence, according to 65 ter, and primarily because the Defence was not informed in good time and adequately. Many issues are raised here - authenticity, time of recording - and there is no explanation why this has not been disclosed to any organisation for ten years, not to the Tribunal. That's why we oppose the admission of this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, this information is in the 65 ter summary, if I may direct Your Honours to a paragraph that says: "After the war the witness returned to Izbica and visited the site. He discovered that during the war the bodies had been removed from the grave-sites." I think that paragraph gives sufficient notice to the fact -- to the evidence that the witness has just given about his return to Izbica. This issue was also discussed with the witness during his examination in the Milutinovic case, and my learned colleague has a copy of the transcript where that is referred to. The witness was specifically asked by the Presiding Judge for this video-tape, and as I had indicated at the start of the session, we had made efforts to obtain it earlier but were unable to do so because it wasn't in the possession of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Anything further, Mr. Djordjevic? The video-clip will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00293, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I had understood that you had nothing further to say when you remained seated, but you were probably reading, Mr. Djordjevic, what was being said. Sorry about that. While we have paused at that point, Ms. Kravetz, can I ask you to clarify one matter which we dealt with a little time ago. That's Exhibit P292, which is the list of bodies that were buried that was prepared by Afrim Xhemajli, if I understood the witness correctly. What we saw on the screen appeared to be only 81 identified bodies. Did we see the full exhibit, or are there more?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If I just may have a moment, Your Honour, and just to indicate, I think Your Honour's referring to Exhibit 2436.01 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm referring to Exhibit P292 in this trial, but you've given the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm informed that the version in e-court is missing a page. The exhibit has two pages, in fact, and it seems that the second page hasn't made it onto e-court. So with your leave, we will seek to rectify that and upload the second page, which is not in the e-court system at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have just been shown the full exhibit, which includes the third column, and the third column contains the missing 46 bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes. My case manager just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I had done my sums, and we had 46 unmentioned, unidentified bodies of the 127 the witness had mentioned. But it's all contained in this third column, so there is no problem anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My case manager just advised me that the full exhibit is in e-court, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness at this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a short break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You would like to go outside for a few moments, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, for two or three minutes. That would be all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness may be shown from the courtroom and brought back as soon as he is available, and while that is happening, Mr. Djordjevic can prepare.
