utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would mention for the transcript that at page 46, lines 20 and 23, Mr. Djordjevic is recorded as having sought a break. It was in fact the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic will now ask some questions of you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Loshi. My name is Dragoljub Djordjevic, Defence attorney for the accused Vlastimir Djordjevic. I just wish to say that Mr. Djordjevic and I are not related. That would not have been allowed according to the code of ethics for Defence counsel before this Tribunal, but still, I wanted to mention it. Now I will ask you some questions as Defence counsel for Mr. Djordjevic concerning your evidence earlier today. We heard when you were born and where you were born. I want to ask you, are you married and do you have children? If so, how many?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm married, and I have three children.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to know if you have a brother or brothers or sisters. How many siblings do you have?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I have one brother and six sisters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to know, is that the brother who you said lived in Kosovska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he, too, a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell me, where did your brother live in 1998 and early 1999?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Up to the moment our house was burnt, we all lived there together. But after our house was burned - and this was sometime in June, I don't remember the date, June 1998 - my brother, my father, my wife, my children, and my mother moved to Prishtina, and they remained there throughout the time when the war ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you graduate from medical school at the university, and where?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I graduated from the faculty of medicine in 1989, in Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When did you find employment after graduation, and where did you work?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I was employed three or four months after I graduated. I graduated in June 1989, and I started working on the 13th of November, 1989, in the clinic in Skenderaj. I worked in the vaccination department and finished the internship that was obligatory. And from there I moved to Runik in 1999 -- correction, 1990. And I worked in Runik ever since. It was an outpatient clinic where I worked throughout this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: May I conclude that you worked until June 1999 in Runik, and which Runik -- or did you continue working until the moment you joined the KLA?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Not in 1999, as you said, but 1998, a year earlier. What you said is correct, so I worked there until 1998 at Runik until sometime in June, and then I went to Leqina and Turiqevc. There was another outpatient clinic if Turiqevc, similar to the one in Runik, and that is where I worked. So we were under the management of the same medical centre of Skenderaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your father, your wife, and three children, if I understood correctly, in June 1998 left Padaliste for the reasons you stated and moved to Kosovska Mitrovica. With whom were they staying there?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: They just over-nighted in Mitrovica. I took them there personally to my uncle's house. The following day, they proceeded for Prishtina, and that's where they lived afterwards. So a day after I took them to Mitrovica in June 1998 - I don't remember the day - they left for Prishtina where they stayed the entire time until the bombing started.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to hear from you where, with whom did they stay in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: They went to Prishtina seeking shelter, like all the other Albanians at that time. At the time they didn't know the owner of the house. There was an emergency group in Prishtina that directed the refugees to households. They lived in the Velanija neighbourhood in Prishtina, in the house of Zanel Sokoli. This was the name of the owner.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next thing I'd like to know is, did you leave after them for Pristina as well?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. What do you mean "after them"? As I said, I took them by car to Mitrovica, and from Mitrovica they went to Prishtina by bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It's perhaps interpretation. I asked you, Did you go with them to Pristina after you spent the night in Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Why did you not go with your family?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I didn't go with them to Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I didn't go with them to Prishtina because there was no need to. I was working as a doctor in the Drenice area. I had my patients, and that was an area where I was the only doctor for some time. There were cases when I have people to assist them when the time was calmer. But when the war escalated, there was no help. So I didn't see any need to accompany them to Prishtina. They just boarded the bus from Mitrovica to Prishtina. However, there was a need for me to take them to Mitrovica because the roads were full of Serb forces, so I didn't want my family to suffer on the check-points of the Serb forces. I'm speaking about the part of the trip to Mitrovica. However, from Mitrovica to Prishtina, there was regular traffic and movement of buses and vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The question I asked you was in fact related to the fact that it's normal for a family member to be with his family, and we'll agree that your family left the place where you lived because of extraordinary circumstances that you claim occurred then. That's why I had asked this question. So you stayed in Lecina, if I'm not mistaken, in the house of a friend, Demush Dragaj; right?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question will be about your friend, Demush Dragaj. Is he related to Shaban Dragaj and Mustafa Dragaj?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No, it's not the same family. I think that Shaban Dragaj and Demush are closer relatives, while Mustafa might be a distant relative. However, Shaban and his family lives in Mitrovica, but earlier his father used to live in Leqina. Shaban didn't live in Leqina. However, Mustafa and Demush lived in Leqina the whole time, but they are not like the same family. They are kind of distant relatives but not the same family.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was Demush Dragaj a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No, he wasn't. Later on when I returned from Tirana to Izbica, when you see me speaking on the tape, the person holding the camera is Demush Dragaj. He had put on the uniform either during the time when I was not in Kosova or after the war. However, during the time I was in Kosova, I didn't see him in uniform. What happened afterwards, that I don't know, I don't have any information about that. But when I returned to Kosova later on, I saw him dressed in a KLA uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: May we then conclude that at that time he was a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: For the time I was in Leqina during the war, he never was a member of the KLA. After the liberation, he had a uniform on, but that does not mean that he was a member of the KLA. Many people used to wear uniforms after the war. He was just a merchant. He supplied the population with food and other goods. Even during the war he was a merchant and he was not involved in the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement of September 2001 you state that you joined the team of medical workers in Turicevac village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 65 ter 2435, a statement from 23rd to 25th September, page 3, para 3; and in B/C/S, it's page 2, para 9, line 3; in Albanian, page 3, para 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me when that happened, that you joined the team of medical workers in Turicevac village?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: As I already mentioned earlier, in June I spoke to the director of the health clinic in Skenderaj and they told me, There's nothing for you to do here; there are no more patients here in the area, so we don't want to you come and work here. At that time I left, the house was burnt down, so the conditions were such that I could not work in Runik anymore. I phoned the director of the clinic in Skenderaj and he said to me that I could work in the clinic of Turiqevc where the medical team was, but there were no other doctors. I was the only doctor. There were medical nurses, medical helpers. There was another custodian, but no other doctor. It seems that when I was working in Runik, no doctor was working in Turiqevc. The population had gone to Izbica and the area surrounding it. So because there were so many people there, it made sense for me to stay there and work as a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to know when that happened.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: In June, June 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Regarding this team, as you call it, of medical workers in Turicevac village, I hear now that you were the only doctor. Did you organise the work of this infirmary or this health centre, or what do you call it, in Turicevac?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that I organised the work. People were working there before. I just went there and started working as a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: At that time did you receive any income for your work in Turicevac?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes. I received my salary, yes, all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: From whom?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I received the salary from the health centre in Skenderaj. I think the payroll was prepared in Mitrovica and then it was sent to Skenderaj and from there to wherever we were working. We were there working under the Serb administration, and that's where I took my salary from.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further in the statement you say, Doctor, that you opened small infirmaries in several villages in that area. Can you tell us in which villages you opened those small infirmaries in the statement that I just quoted?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes. In Leqina where I was living, in the order of Demush Dragaj, I worked from there. I had some medicaments in that place. There was a medical worker working with me at the time. Another centre was at the house of Zaim Bajrami, who I mentioned earlier. He worked in Izbica. So these were the two places where we had the health centres. I wouldn't call them clinics, just small centres. There was one in Turiqevc, and they were there to help people, patients mostly, who were forced to move from one area to another. We had to be there to offer our help as doctors.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly that even after that you remained the only doctor in that area?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes. I would say I was the only doctor. Later on, another doctor came. He was not working for the health centre, but he wanted to work. He had graduated during the time when we had problems with the Serb administration, in those ten years. I won't mention here all the problems we had. So this doctor had not graduated during the time that the Serb administration was in full force in Kosova. He had graduation -- had graduated during the time that we had conflicts with Kosova -- with the Serbian government, and his diploma was not recognized. But he wanted to work and offer his help at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What was the name of your colleague?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Fatmir Fazliu, and he was killed later by the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me as far as Mr. Fatmir Fazliu is concerned, before he died you said that he worked as a doctor; is that right? And did he receive any kind of a salary or remuneration? Apparently, it was not from the Serbian government for the work that he did.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No, Fatmir did not receive any money. He just was willing to work as a volunteer, and he was not paid for what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Where was he from, if you know? Could you tell us, where did he live?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: He was from Turiqevc, lived in Turiqevc. He was the only son of Bajram. His father was called Bajram, meaning Bajram Fazliu.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me, so we're talking about the village of Turicevac. This is where this clinic or infirmary was that you set up, or, rather, that you said you joined the medical team that was providing medical services there. At that time when you came to Turicevac and from that moment on, how were you able to obtain drugs and medical supplies that were necessary to provide medical services to the population?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: We did communicate with a health centre in Skenderaj, and that's where we got the medical supplies from; for example, syringes and injections, and also tourniquets to dress wounds and so on. Part of the medical supplies came from international humanitarian organisations, such as CARE, but there were other organisations as well whose names I can't remember now. So we were supplied with medication both by the health centre in Skenderaj and the humanitarian organisations. Sometimes these organisations provided medical workers as well to help us and the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you two more questions about Turicevac. The first one is: did your team of medical workers, the team that you worked with, provide medical assistance to the members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My second question: Did your medical team in Turicevac treat members of other ethnic communities, including Serbs?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: There were no Serbs in Turiqevc. This is an area where Serbs have never lived. I've never heard of any Serbs living in Turiqevc.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The reason why I ask you this is because I know, it's my personal knowledge, that among members of other ethnic communities there were numerous refugees. And if some of them had been in that area, that is why I asked you this. So no, your answer is no; is that correct? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, I will have to apologise to the Trial Chamber. I provided the wrong reference in the transcript that I referred to from the 65 ter. It's not 2435 but 2536, page 10 in the English version and page 5 in the Albanian version. So I will now continue with my questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. You asked the question and did not allow me to answer. You said that there were other refugees there from other ethnicities. I did not answer that question. I'm saying that there were no refugees from other ethnicities there. We helped everybody who was there. If there had been any Serbs there, I would have helped them as well. I have treated Serbs in Runik and wherever I worked. I went to their homes. I had good relations with them as a doctor. However, during the war, as I said, I went to Turiqevc, and when I worked in Turiqevc, there were no Serbs there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. My next question pertains to the fact that you said that from June 1998 you worked using your mobile phone as a reporter for an Albanian TV station, TV-SH, from the area of Izbica. In your statement from September 2001, you say that you worked for that radio station, and in the statement that you gave in the Milosevic case, in the evidence that you gave at page, I think, 9441, paragraphs 13 and 14, you say that you worked as a reporter for Kosovo Television. Now, let us clear this up. Did you report for the TV-SH, an Albanian station, for the Kosovo station, or for both TV channels? Could you please tell us, what is the correct version?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: The correct version is, and the truth is because there are no versions, that I worked voluntarily for the Kosova Radio and Television - that was based in Tirana - not for the TV-SH. Because the premises of the Kosova Television were occupied by Serb forces, the workers had left the place and had gone to Albania. People who worked there in Prishtina were lackeys of Milosevic, so we did not cooperate with that office. In Tirana, there was the Kosova Radio and Television office. They had a half-an-hour news edition every day. I cooperated with them. I helped them but as a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. A volunteer. That means that you were not paid. Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No, I was not paid.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 19th of May, 1999, you gave a statement to an investigator of this Tribunal in Tirana, and you confirmed on that occasion that the statement had been read out to you in the Albanian language and that it contained everything that you recounted, to the best of your knowledge and recollection. Do you remember whether you signed each and every page of the statement that you gave in Tirana? That's the 19th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In the statement at page 2, paragraph 3, in the B/C/S version - it's the same reference in the Albanian language - you said yesterday: "On the 18th of May, 1999, I visited the office of the ICTY in Tirana, Albania, and to Jonathan Tait-Harris, one of the investigators, I handed over the original version of the video-tape that I used when I recorded the aftermath of what I would call the massacre in Izbica."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, I will read more slowly. Should I repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday: "On the 18th of May, 1999, I visited the office of the ICTY in Tirana, Albania, and I gave an investigator, Jonathan Tait-Harris, the original version of the video-type I used when I recorded the after-math of what I will call the massacre in Izbica." And then at the same page, paragraph 2; 6 in the B/C/S language, you say: "I made the video-tape myself. I recorded it myself on the 31st of March, 1999, and this is the original copy that has been in my possession from the time when I recorded it until now." The reference for the pages is the same in the English and the Albanian versions. Now, my question to you is: Why didn't you say then that it was actually recorded by your friend, Sefedin Thaqi, and you did not even mention his name on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I don't remember why I did not tell him. It seems I said that I made the recording; however, I considered that that was mainly what I had done. In the socialist times, we were used to this idea that the journalist goes with the cameraman. And the journalist is responsible for everything. The cameraman does whatever the journalist tells him to do. However, later on, when they asked me more detailed questions, I explained how the situation was. As you can see, this is a very short statement, the one that was given at the time. There was no special reason why I did not provide the name of Sefedin Thaqi at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do I understand it correctly that the same reasons were behind what you said in the statement that you gave on the 23rd and the 25th of September, 2001, where you say, "My part of the video-recording begins with the men digging the trenches in Izbica on the 31st of March, 1999." And it reads, 00600; the English is at page 6, para 8, and the Albanian, page 6, para 5. And you said that it was your recording, although you knew at the time that you did not actually record the footage. Were you prompted by the same reasons again?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No. There is another reason. Sefedin Thaqi left his home. At his home he had a relative who had been killed, and he recorded his trip to Izbica. I wanted the camera and the tape to record the massacre in Izbica. That's why the cassette that I provided begins with the graves being opened, being dug in Izbica. I did not mention there the part that Sefedin Thaqi had recorded on his own when I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now tell us what happened to Mr. Sefedin Thaqi? Where is he today? Is he still alive? What he's doing, what he was doing at the time, just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Sefedin Thaqi at the time was working as a teacher. He worked in a school. He was a civilian all the time. He never was a member of the KLA. I think he's alive, and he must be working as a teacher in Kosova. I'm not sure because I don't live in Kosova now. When I go to Kosova, I try to meet as many people as possible, the ones that I know, my relatives and so on. I met him once, and as far as I know he still works as a teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let me move on to the part that was dealt with by my colleague Ms. Kravetz at the end of your examination-in-chief. That's the list of the bodies that was done by Afrim Xhemajli, as you told us. Is it true that Afrim gave you the list of the bodies that he made, actually, that he did it when the bodies were buried?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the counsel please repeat the date when the list was handed over to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In mid-April 1999.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in fact your first contact with the investigators of this Tribunal happened on the 19th of May, 1999, in Tirana?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Why did you not hand this list over during the first contact that you had with the investigators of the Tribunal, in other words, on the 19th of May, 1999? Because we can see from your previous answer that you had had this list for a month before that, and let me remind you that you did it three days later.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Could you clarify it? I do have an answer, but I think I want a clearer question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, why didn't you hand the list over, the list of persons identified -- who were identified and who had allegedly died in the massacre that was perpetrated by the Serbian forces in the village of Izbica?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I met Jonathan Harris and gave him the tape. This was the first meeting. You're saying the 18th. I accept it. It must have been the 18th. However, I did not have the list on me on that day. I think I went back the next day and I met another investigator, because I had promised Jonathan that I would bring the list but I did not have it on me when I met Jonathan. So I think the next day I met another investigator; his name was Kevin, and I gave the list to him. There was no other reason. It was simply because the list was in the place where I was living and I did not have it on me when I met Jonathan. I mentioned the list and I said to them, to Jonathan, that I will bring it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I will have to go back to the issue of Sefedin Thaqi, the teacher who actually recorded the footage of what you say was based on your ideas and the way you asked him to. Why is it that it took you two years -- that you told investigators, I think it was in the Canada at the Royal Canadian Mounted Police headquarters, why did it take you two years to say that it was -- that you told Sefedin Thaqi to do that?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: As I explained earlier when I gave my statement in Tirana, that was a very short statement. The investigator didn't ask me many questions, so we left it to that, the short statement, as you can see. However, the other investigator, Malvin Dagsland, who came to Canada, he stayed there for a longer time, asked me detailed questions, and I answered his questions. So in providing him with a detailed answer, I also provided him with this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Djordjevic, for a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will agree with you. It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will have the second break now and resume at five minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will now continue where I left off. A few brief questions on your statement -- rather, on your evidence earlier today. You said you had joined the KLA and you stated why and when. There is a passage in your earlier testimony in the Milosevic case and the Milutinovic case, as well, especially the part when they asked you: Is it true you were a local commander of the KLA? And I mean Padaliste. And I don't think that comment is correct, but I'll have to ask you once again. Do you stand by that statement that you had never been a commander or anything like that even on a local level in the KLA?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by that statement. I don't remember ever saying that or someone ever asking me about that. But if this is your question, my answer is no, I never was a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Considering that you are a doctor and that Kosovo is, subjectively speaking, a very small area, I suppose you knew other people in your profession, both Serbian and Albanian and maybe of other ethnicities, working in Kosovo. Would I be right?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes. Not that many were doctors because there weren't many doctors. In Drenice, there were not so many -- there was no single Serbian doctor. A nurse came later. She worked in the village of Banja that was inhabited by Serbs, but she worked there for quite some short time. I just met her once, perhaps. But as for other medical staff, yes, I did have contacts of this kind, and I knew these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: To be quite clear, I was asking you about doctors working in Kosovo, physicians working in Kosovo at the time. Did you know your colleagues, I mean, in Pristina, in Mitrovica, Srbica, Pec, other towns in Kosovo? Did you know your colleagues, doctors?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to know if you know, and I can see that you are rather well informed, do you know that two of your colleagues, Albanian doctors, were killed in the summer of 1998 in Pec? Do you know about that case?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: In Peja?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Two ethnic Albanian doctors, your colleagues, medical doctors, do you know about that case?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: It is possible that I've heard of this, but currently I don't remember. If you give me their names, maybe I can help. As I said, I might have had this information in the past, but I also mentioned that I lived in an area where the fighting was more intensive, developments were more intensive. However, I don't remember this event in Peja.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to tell you their names. I'm just going to say they are your colleagues, ethnic Albanians, because you said a moment ago you knew all doctors in Kosovo. So I'm surprised you didn't hear about this case, when KLA members killed those two colleagues of yours in the summer of 1998 because they had refused to join the movement. We will present evidence before this Court concerning this case but not today. I'm rather surprised, as I said, that you have not heard of this incident, which is unusual. Doctors are not killed every day, especially at that time.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: It might sound unusual, but I really don't remember this. And when you say that the KLA killed them, I think that this was part of the propaganda that was launched at that time. I worked as a local doctor and I didn't have information about what was going on in other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to question you anymore about this or draw conclusions because that's not my job. My next question has to do with members of the KLA. Did members of the KLA wear uniforms constantly or not? Were they sometimes in mufti?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: We should explain this issue in broader terms. A short answer would be that some soldiers, a part of soldiers had uniforms and some others didn't. Some who had uniforms would not wear them at all times. Why? Because they would pass in more dangerous areas where they could be spotted by the Serb forces, or they would, for that matter, make the Serb forces occupy that area and retaliate with the Serbian population. So some soldiers did have uniforms; some didn't. In broader terms, since it was impossible for all the KLA soldiers to have uniforms - this is due to financial reasons; there weren't enough funds to provide each and every member with a weapon and a uniform - so my answer would be that almost half of the KLA did not have uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you say that nevertheless those who did not wear uniforms and were still members of the KLA wore some emblems that made them recognisable to other members of the KLA, be it in actions or in areas where the KLA had control? If there were such markings or emblems, what were they?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Those who had uniforms had the KLA emblem. I think they wore it on their right shoulder or left; that I don't know. And those who didn't have uniforms, they didn't have any emblems or symbols on them to identify them as members. They would wear civilian clothes. Some would have weapons, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that there was a danger that during street-to-street fighting between members of the KLA and what you refer to as Serb forces, members of the KLA who were not clearly identified and who were not known to uniformed KLA members could be injured or even killed in such fighting in which they participated, either carrying weapons or not?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: There was no danger of this kind. The KLA was organised into units, and usually those who wore uniforms moved together with those who didn't have uniforms. So there weren't such groups that were outside any command, that could do whatever they pleased, and that could not identify other members. This was impossible, because even if a member did not have a uniform, he would be part of a unit that contained soldiers with uniforms. And this unit would have a commander and everybody was held responsible before this commander. On the other side, there weren't open conflicts between the Serb forces and the KLA in the area where I was active as a doctor, so this possibility was non-existent in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, speaking of uniforms, you, personally, as a member of the KLA, were you more often in uniform than not?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Most of the time I worked as a doctor, and during my work in the outpatient clinic until 3 p.m., I would not wear a uniform. Every now and then, out of my own wish, I would put on the uniform because somehow it helped to raise the level of morale among the population and among other soldiers. So I would wear the uniform when we spoke to the people, where we had gatherings, on these occasions. I was issued with a uniform. Although it was difficult to get a uniform, I was offered one and I accepted it with pleasure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that on the 29th of March, in Tusilje there were members of the KLA who had stayed there to take care of their families. Were they wearing uniforms then?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No, they weren't. In other words, they could have gone to the spot wearing uniforms, but those who had uniforms had returned and those who had weapons had returned, and those who had remained there, they were without a weapon and without uniforms. So on the day when the Serb forces entered and gathered a part of the civilian population, there were KLA members amongst them and they were later released, either because the Serbian authorities didn't have information on these people. But they were released together with the civilian population. There were about 50 of them who were together with the civilian population and who were later released.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I made a certain conclusion, and I'd like to ask you if I'm correct. From what we've just heard from you, I infer that the members of the KLA very frequently mixed with the civilians, and it was sometimes impossible to know who were civilians and who were members of the KLA. Would it be true to say that members of the KLA blended with the civilians so that they were not identifiable to those who did not know these people? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Partly, I would say. When there were internal movements of the population, the soldiers would accompany them to another area. Some would remain with the civilian population, but the majority of them would withdraw. So there wasn't a mixture of that great extent, as you say. The soldiers would help their own families to move from one location to another, and then most of them would withdraw and go to their original units or locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: While we are still on the subject of uniforms, you mentioned Serb forces. I'd like to know if you distinguish between the army and the police, and I mean in particular insignia, colour, appearance of the uniform. If you know the difference between the two, can you explain what the difference is?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I was a member of the army. I completed the service, so I know that they wear green uniforms. When I say "member," I said member of the JNA. I've also seen the uniforms of the Serb police while I resided there. It's a uniform of a greyish dark blue colour. Maybe I'm not that clear, but this was the difference between the two types of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What about vehicles?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell the difference. They are of different colours. The vehicles of the police were always blue, to my recollection, dark blue, while the military vehicles were green.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your evidence today you mentioned tanks. What colour were the tanks?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Green, the one that I saw, the one that was moving from Turiqevc in the direction of Runik, the one that I saw in the morning of the 30th of May, 1999. It was early in the morning, and this tank was green. On the same day yet later, I saw other vehicles, and what I remember best was this tank, another tank of the same colour, and a truck, also green colour. They were at Vojnik, and they were moving in the direction of Turiqevc and Broja. So I waited for these vehicles to move and then for me to go to Izbica. When I was sure that there were no longer Serb forces there, I set off, and from Kopiliq through Vojnik I went to Izbica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we then conclude that those were military vehicles?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes. On the 30th of April, the ones that I saw were military vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that on the 30th of March in the evening, Tusilje was shelled and some people were killed. As a result, some people were arrested. First of all, I have to ask you where you have this information from and who were the people who were arrested, if you know? Who arrested them, if they were indeed arrested? And do you know the reasons? Perhaps this is a compound question, so I'll stop here.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: This is what I heard from others. Around 50 or 60 persons were arrested, maybe even more. I don't remember the exact figure, but I think about 50 or 60 were arrested and taken to the police station in Skenderaj. So since they were taken to the police station, it was the Serb police that arrested them. Later on I spoke with some of the people who had been arrested. So they were arrested in Tushile by the Serbian police. At the same time the army was also present there in Tushile, and even some civilians said that some army members treated the population very well. I heard of a case when a young Serbian soldier cried because of the situation that the civilians were in. I heard of some figures, that 11 people had been killed and stuff like that, but I cannot confirm the veracity of this information. Your question -- second question was why they were arrested; this I don't know. Why they were released; this I don't know either. This is an issue of the Serbian security services. I know that amongst those who had been released there were KLA members. I still don't know why they were released, whether they didn't have information on them. This I don't know. But the fact is that they were released and I don't know any more details about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that you heard but that you cannot confirm the figure of 11 people who were killed. I now want to ask you this: Were they killed in the shelling or were they murdered? What happened?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I heard that they were killed during the shelling, but maybe this information was not very accurate because there were killed people but not as many as they said. Later on I moved on from that area, and I haven't been able since to ascertain what the number was. I heard that there was a smaller number of people that were killed, two or three or so, but there was no execution. So nothing like what happened in Izbica happened in Tushile. There was no execution, summary execution, by firearms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We will agree that you did not witness that event. You were telling us what you heard from those other persons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes. I only saw the forces accompanying the civilian population, but I was not present at the area at that time. I did not see the killings. I did not see any bodies in Tushile.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can we also agree that the 30th of March is the day when you saw, as you say in your statement and confirm here, that from Gornji Obilic on that day green trucks were moving and Serb tanks, I think you mentioned, up to Vojnika, the Vojnika hill.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes. From the Vojnik hill I saw the tanks and some vehicles, not many of them. They were staying there during the morning and a little later as well. Later on they moved on to Broja and Turiqevc.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question: Are you sure that all those civilians - the majority of them were let go and you say that there were KLA members among them - so that all of those civilians were arrested or taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. I'm not clear. I don't see the logic. Is it sure that everybody was arrested? I can't understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I'm not sure that you received the proper interpretation. I asked you -- well, first of all, let me ask you this: Do you see the difference between being arrested and being taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes. These people were arrested but not imprisoned. They were held; I don't know for how long, maybe two or three hours, maybe half a day, but later on they were all released. At least that was the information that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will not dwell on this issue or ask any more questions. My next question: You claim that on the 20th of March, 1999 -- the date changed to the 29th of March after your testimony in the Milosevic case. So we have first the 20th of March, that's in your statement, and in the Milosevic case you testified that it was on the 29th of March. So the members of the Serb army and police and paramilitaries surrounded Srbica, all together, and that in the course of those operations some 16 civilians were killed, you provide that exact figure, in the town itself. First of all, did you see that with your own eyes? Are you an eye-witness? That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I will first answer the first question you asked. I never said the 29th. You might have a look again at my statement. I always said the 20th and never the 29th. And also, I was not an eye-witness of what happened. This is what I heard from other people, the patients who came to me who had been injured. I was working in Turiqevc, I gave them first aid, and they gave me the names of the people who had died. I had the list. We went to identify 14 people there, and when I reported for the Kosova Radio and Television, I gave the names of the people who were killed on the 20th of March, 1999, in Skenderaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So I will conclude that the date that we were talking about is definitely the 20th of March, 1999. Thank you. Now, as regards Srbica, were there any direct -- was there any direct fighting there between the Serb forces and the so-called Kosovo Liberation Army?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: I'm not aware that there have been fightings, direct fightings. This was also suggested to me by Milosevic himself and the Milutinovic Defence, but I stand by the information I received at the time, that there was not any confrontation going on between the KLA and the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Do you know that on the 20th of March, 1999, at 5 a.m., members of the KLA attacked the police station in Srbica and that a police officer, Zoran Rakocevic, died of his injuries, the injuries he sustained in the attack? He did not die the very same day but the next day in the Pristina hospital. Another police officer, Zoran Gemajlovic, was wounded in the attack. Or to put it quite simply, do you know that one Serb police officer was killed on that occasion and another seriously wounded?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No, no, because as I told you, I did not know of any confrontations between KLA and the Serb forces. There were policemen who were going from house to house, bringing the people out and executing some of them. Some of these people are still missing. From a family, 16 people are still missing to this day. This was suggested to me even in the previous trials when I testified. I don't know how the media -- the Serb media covered that story or where they got it from, but I think it's not possible. I was not there. I did not see anything like that. That is the truth. I'm giving comments here on the basis of what I heard from people who came from the place it happened, in Skenderaj. Part of them went to Turiqevc; part of them went to Izbica where most of the civilians were. Some of them I treated because they had bruises; they had wounds on their faces, legs, and arms. I treated them and while I was treating them, I asked them what happened and they told me. When I'm saying that the KLA was not doing anything -- was not active in the area, I asked people from the KLA what the developments were and I reported the information they gave to me to the Kosova Radio and Television. So I did not have any such information that an attack of that sort happened in Skenderaj on the 20th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that on the 20th of March, 1999, you were still a doctor employed by the medical centre in Srbica, so for all intents and purposes you worked in Runik, as you told us, but you were paid by the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I can't remember when the salary was suspended, and it was not a big amount of money. I can't remember the last salary I received and when I received it. I'm not sure. I don't remember when the last time was that I was paid.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: But we will agree that you were still employed by the medical centre in Srbica, the 20th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was employed by the medical centre in Skenderaj all the time, and I never resigned from that job officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And you still worked in Runik at that time.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No, no. In Turiqevc, not in Runik. As I said, I left Runik earlier, a year earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What's the name of the director of the medical centre, or, rather, what was his name on the 20th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: The director of the medical centre in Skenderaj was called Nexhmedin Hoti. There was another department in Mitrovica where the general director was. He was a Serb. I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't care about the general director. What is important for me is whether you were in contact with your director or manager in Srbica.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any contact. There was no need to. Whenever they could, they sent us supplies of medications but not direct contact. I did not go to Skenderaj because I thought I was at risk from the Serb forces. I was a well-known person in the area. I was operating -- I was working in the area where there was fighting, so I did not go to Skenderaj. There was one contact only when we agreed that I would continue to work, but that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We will agree, Dr. Loshi, that you, as a reporter of the KLA, were not told by the KLA about its great success in the action in Srbica, and we will agree that your director failed to inform you about the medical response or treatment that was given to those three police officers after they were wounded.

utterances.speaker: LIRI LOSHI
utterances.text: Yes, I agree that I was not given this information by anybody ever, and that's the reason why I think it did not happen. Maybe they were killed somewhere else in another development but then it was ascribed to Skenderaj so that they would justify the police operation. But I believe that did not happen in Skenderaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Djordjevic? We've gone overtime.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the next set of questions would go beyond the temporal frame-work that has to do with our trial today, so I think this would really be a very good moment for me to stop my cross-examination for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We must finish now to allow another Chamber to continue in the courtroom. We'll resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 10th day of February, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
